summary: Defines a device value for the vCard KIND property so vCard can describe computing devices such as servers, routers, switches, printers, sensors and phones, not just people and organizations.

eli5.summary: A contact card normally describes a person. This lets a card describe a machine, such as a printer, instead.

questions: can a vcard describe a device
how do device vcards link to other vcards
subtitle: Lets a vCard describe a computing device, such as a router or printer, instead of a person or organization.

tldr.problem: vCard 4 could say whether a card describes an individual, organization, group, location or application, but had no way to mark a card as describing a computing device.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the value device for the vCard KIND property and shows how device cards can carry properties like FN, URL and GEO and link to related cards using RELATED.
tldr.outcome: Devices can carry or publish their own vCards for asset tracking and operations. The RFC warns that publishing device details can help attackers find vulnerable devices.

today: RFC 6869 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata. It builds on RFC 6350, and complements RFC 6473.

sections.title: Why a Device Kind
sections.content:
Version 4 of vCard (RFC 6350) has a KIND property saying what type of entity a card represents. The VCARDDAV Working Group defined the values individual, org, group and location. A more general thing was considered, but it was decided to split it into software applications and hardware devices, and only application was defined at the time (RFC 6473).

Since then, use cases for device vCards have emerged: using vCards as a primer for inventory and asset tracking data specific to network elements. This document therefore adds the value device. It is limited to computing devices, which makes it distinct from purely mechanical devices such as elevators or electric generators that cannot communicate over a network. Network-attached sensors on such machines are not excluded.
sections.eli5: Cards already existed for people, companies, groups and places. This adds one more kind for computers and gadgets that connect to a network.

sections.title: What Counts as a Device
sections.content:
When KIND is device, the vCard represents a computing device such as an appliance, computer or network element, for example a server, router, switch, printer, sensor or phone. The RFC says this is functionally equivalent to the device object class in LDAP (RFC 4519), but a device here can also be virtual, such as a virtual machine running inside another physical element.

A vCard can be embedded into a device at manufacturing time so that basic information such as the serial number, support email and documentation URL is available at initial deployment. It can be modified after deployment to hold user-specified data, so the data serves both asset tracking and operational purposes.

A finer-grained taxonomy, such as a subtype of router or computer, is explicitly out of scope.
sections.eli5: A device card can describe a real machine or a pretend one living inside another computer. The maker can put the basics on the card, and the owner can add more later.

sections.title: Several Cards per Device
sections.content:
A device might have several embedded vCards for different purposes. How to discover and access them is deliberately left unspecified. Example cards the RFC lists: the device itself, the organization or person that makes it, a person or role that maintains it, and application-level vCards (RFC 6473) for each installed application.

On the device's own card, FN might carry the hostname, URL a documentation website, KEY a certificate provisioned at manufacture, and ADR, GEO and TZ the physical address, location and time zone.

The device card can link to the other cards with the RELATED property, which makes it easy to tell the device's card from those of the vendor, administrator and applications. The other cards need not point back.
sections.eli5: One machine can have a small stack of cards: one for itself, one for who built it, one for who looks after it. The machine's card points to the others.

sections.title: Example and IANA Registration
sections.content:
The example is a router described in the XML form of vCard (xCard, RFC 6351). It mixes manufacturing details with post-deployment attributes, points to a related administrative contact with RELATED, and uses xCard extension namespaces for extras such as a serial number, MAC address and software version.

IANA added the value device for the KIND property to the vCard Property Values table in the vCard Elements registry. The registration states that the entity represented is a computing device such as an appliance, computer or network element.
sections.eli5: The example is a card for a router listing its name, support contact and location. A central list was updated so everyone recognizes the new kind of card.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Registering the value does not by itself add security considerations beyond those in RFC 6350. However, risks can arise for vulnerable Internet-connected devices when identification details from device vCards are published. Well-known, publicly accessible device vCard repositories can raise the chance that an existing vulnerability is exploited, especially for devices with no good way to update software or firmware.

It is the device administrator's responsibility to follow best current security practices and to apply upgrades and patches. Specifications defining device-specific vCard extensions or profiles also need to consider this increased risk.
sections.eli5: If a card tells the whole world exactly what machine you have, a bad person can look for known weak spots. So keep your machines up to date.
